Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy.

Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a regression network to predict projection grouping from the object's raw image. Next, we train a corresponding branch that generates corresponding points from the object's 3D model based on the learned projection grouping. We then combine both branches to derive the object's pose by formulating an optimization problem. Experiments conducted on the IMWOCA and CO3D datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Notably, it notably surpassed the current state-of-the-art by a margin of 14.12% in terms of AP when evaluating indoor object poses.

challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has since expanded to encompass
extensions such as nested and weighted variants, as well as adaptations for
time-series data, wavelets, and more. The underlying problem's convexity has
allowed the development of multiple solution methods, both generic and tailored

alongside four solution methods: Tailored ADMM, General ADMM, Coordinated Descent,
and Chordal Decomposition. The library features ready-to-use implementations for
multivariate and time-series data, providing both basic and customized data
constructs to easily integrate new variants and algorithms. GGLasso has been
tested on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness
of our implementations. The library is now freely accessible on GitHub at

Abstract:

Acoustic lenses made of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) were tested to see if they could improve the detection sensitivity of hydrophones by focusing high-frequency sound waves. The hydrophones used in this study had a small diameter and low electrical power consumption. To test the optical lens efficiency, two different lens designs were fabricated and placed between the transducer and water. As a result, one lens design produced a signal strength of -2.8 dB and another produced 39.5 dB, which could significantly improve the detection capabilities of the hydrophones. These findings suggest that using PMMA lenses could make it possible for highly sensitive detection at low frequencies.

This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the splash dome closing due to its natural shrinkage to closing due to merging of coalescing surfaces, along with the development of internal currents within the formed cavity that could have implications for underwater entry of objects, such as space debris, satellites, and missiles.

We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory.

A new hardware and software attack targets the security module's ability to isolate threats by poisoning its resources. Instead of directly modifying security settings, the attacker exploits available storage and CPU capacity to manipulate the security module's priority scheduling. 

If configured with the same security module, the attacker then gains control over mobile devices used to distribute malware-infused applications. Instead of forcing the security module to accept malicious code, they adjust device configuration to prioritize their app, effectively displacing it from the security module and gaining total device control. 

Furthermore, with only one security module dominating the market on popular mobile devices, users' lack of choice makes it difficult to avoid this attack, especially given its reliance on legitimate storage modification.

The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. We examine the impact of using beam splitters versus parametric amplifiers on the production of SPCCSs, focusing on the success probabilities of the process, the photon number statistics, and quadrature fluctuations. CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical workflow by comparing the performance of tumor detection methods trained solely on CT scans to those trained on a multi-source dataset. To accomplish this, we created a dataset called CEsTIA consisting of over 1000 cases with annotations from multiple sources including CT scans, endoscopic images, medical histories, and surgical reports. We demonstrate that training methods exclusively on CT scans from this dataset result in comparable tumor-detection rates to those trained on the multi-source data. Our analysis indicates that our proposed approach can lead to a more efficient and less cumbersome clinical workflow.

One area of improvement lies in optimizing hydraulic fracturing, but this task is complicated due to the interacting forces between fluid injection and rock breakdown.  A new study investigates how to model these interactions in three-dimensional, multi-stage scenarios, which is crucial for designing effective stimulation jobs. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as contributing equally, neither serving as nor being hindered by a source or target domain. Consequently, each domain contributes a unique and unique preference profile to the recommendation process. To achieve this, we devise a unified factor model and a neural network-based model to capture domain-specific preferences and facilitate domain interaction, respectively. Further, we design a self-supervised contrastive learning strategy to enhance the model's performance. Comprehensive experiments conducted on three real-world datasets underscore the superiority of our proposed MSDCR framework over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR baselines.

While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. These clusters exhibit a unique and complex motion within a two-dimensional lattice, contrasting with isolated, site-based interactions where particles move freely, independently. Instead, in systems exhibiting this cluster motion behavior, an over-damped dynamic results, with clusters that move slowly, accompanied by an internal reorganization. This simultaneous occurrence of complex internal reorganization and slow external movement gives rise to an additional degree of freedom, which could be utilized for both information and energy processing. Particularly in models featuring the extended-Hubbard interaction, a unique multi-time scale emerges, with fast internal dynamics and slower external movements, providing the necessary conditions for distinct separation of spatial and temporal variables. This separation is a crucial component in the operation of thermodynamic engines. Consequently, these self-organizing clusters have the potential to serve as functional components in 2D lattices that host both moving and stationary sub-systems, which could underlie active matter and living organisms.

Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to create new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a B-Tree variant to build conflict-resolved copies of mutable data, enabling efficient and conflict-free operations. the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered.

To explore the possibility of using this test, the velocity distribution in the outer regions of the Milky Way was analyzed using data on star systems from the Gaia Tenth Data Release. The velocity distribution was examined in a cylindrical coordinate system, with the origin at the center of the Milky Way, and was divided into thin cylindrical shells with heights equal to their radii. The velocity dispersion within each shell was calculated, and the results were compared to two testable predictions derived from the Modified Newtonian Dynamics theory, as well as the standard gravitational model. The analysis indicated that the velocity dispersion in the Milky Way's disk conforms to the predicted $a$ pattern of the Modified Newtonian Dynamics theory, but deviates from both the standard gravitational model and the prediction of the $\sqrt{a}$ pattern. Additionally, the result may also be influenced by the relative influence of the galaxy's disk and halo components.

It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory, finding applications in the analysis of nucleic acid sequences, protein folding, and the classification of closed loops in a three-dimensional space, represented by the fundamental group of that space. This paper introduces a novel type of unknotting operation, called diagonal move, specifically for the study of oriented, labeled knots and links. The new operation is shown to be effective in transforming any knot diagram into a trivial unknot, provided the sequence of moves is complemented with the traditional moves, including rotation and crossing changes.

problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning rely heavily on matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used operation, can pose performance bottlenecks if not optimized. This is particularly evident when dealing with large and sparse matrices, which are often encountered in graph-based applications. While several techniques have been developed to enhance the optimization of general matrix multiplication, including OAI and GTM, their applicability to sparse matrices is limited. In response, we have introduced a new algorithm, the Binary Tree Method (BTM), another form of parallel matrix multiplication. BTM has several key benefits, including simplicity, ease of implementation, and minimal communication requirements. We have also evaluated BTM in conjunction with existing techniques and have demonstrated its vast potential in improving performance for various types of computations, including graph-based applications and machine learning models like BGL, Node2Vec, and Facebook's DeepInfo. To further validate these findings, we have utilized multiple hardware configurations, including CPU and GPU, and have showcased BTM's superior performance over traditional methods, such the GNU Scientific Library and cuSPARSE, in a wide range of test cases.

We examine the role of two-loop electroweak corrections to Higgs production via the vector-boson fusion process, using recent new-logarithmic calculations for the relevant Green's functions at the same order. Vector-boson fusion accounts for nearly half of total Higgs-production cross-section at the LHC and colliders with center-of-mass energies from 150 GeV to 8 TeV, making it a pivotal process. It contributes significantly to the total cross-section in the low-mass Higgs-regime, particularly in the regime where the Higgs boson mass is less than 120 GeV, necessitating precise control of quantum corrections, specifically two-loop electroweak ones, to experimentally confirm the Standard Model Higgs boson at the future high-luminosity LHC. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients primarily relies on heart volume and function as per existing medical guidelines. The best indicators for these factors are found through 3D image analysis of the heart obtained from magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging. Recent research involving a type of neural network known as U-Net has yielded promising initial results when tested against heart images derived from CT scans. However, applying this approach to PV replacement surgery timing requires enhanced validation using high-quality CMR images, along with relevant clinical data. This research involved validating the model using 140 such images from 80 patients with TOF, combined with their corresponding clinical records. Results showed that using two metrics derived from analysis (right ventricle volume and a related index) allowed for accurate prediction of the stage of heart condition with an overall accuracy of around 75%. While this prediction could support clinical decision-making, it was found to be inconsistent with current clinical practices. Therefore, further testing using larger datasets is needed to enhance model reliability, ultimately aiding clinicians in providing personalized medical advice for these patients through the use of artificial intelligence.

Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting feature accumulation for large-scale objects and triggering dimension regression. To address this, we propose two novel large-object-oriented architectures called Large-Object Feature Pyramid Networks (LO-FPNs): Balanced FPN (BFPN) and Unified-Branch FPN (UB-FPN). BFPN modulates feature branch weights to equalize gradient flows, whereas UB-FPN introduces an extra unified branch to enhance feature integration. Empirical evaluations on the COCO benchmark demonstrate BFPN's compatibility with various detector types and indicate that UB-FPN outperforms the original FPN framework by a notable margin of 1.4% mAP.

Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected as a result of removing one node. In the context of tree-like networks, this paper derives exact mathematical expressions for the expected number of nodes that become disconnected when a node is removed. It also explores the distribution of nodes that become disconnected in large trees and presents numerical simulations to validate the findings. increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for the implementation of IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on a radar system equipped with an IRS that modulates polarization. We investigate the effects of incorporating IRS technology on radar target detection, range estimation, Doppler estimation, and polarization estimation. Our findings reveal significant improvements in signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR), range and Doppler resolution, and polarization estimation accuracy when using the IRS-based radar system. We demonstrate substantial gains of up to $12$ dB in SINR, as well as up to $77.4\%$ improvement in polarization estimation accuracy. These results highlight the potential of the proposed IRS-based radar technology to enhance radar performance.

A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. These methods have their own advantages, but they also have limitations. We show that TGDC yields the best results in the continual learning benchmark, significantly outperforming the baseline models and existing state-of-the-art methods by a large margin.

ysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty also extends to observing the end states, especially when they occur outside of binary interactions, such as the death of a massive star or the collision of a compact object with a non-compact object. To efficiently perform these calculations for large numbers of systems, we have created the Python module `common_envelope.py`, which can also be used for both specific cases and broader binary population synthesis studies, as it incorporates the necessary input files and utilizes parts of the `bse` code for broader applications. This module allows researchers to easily access the light curves, end states, and other properties of various binary star interactions, as it has already been populated with existing data from previous calculations, which can be accessed through its built-in functions.

or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this limitation. Firstly, collecting remote objects is difficult because most objects visible from afar are small and hard to spot, requiring high-resolution imaging which is expensive. Secondly, annotating such objects is laborious and relies on the collaboration of multiple people, making it impractical for large-scale datasets. To tackle these challenges, we introduce a novel dataset collection tool called FarFieldAnnotator, along with a comprehensive evaluation pipeline to analyze far-field detection performance. Moreover, we believe far-field detection is crucial for the development of fully autonomous vehicles. To move the field forward, we release our FarFieldDetector baseline and establish the $\textsc{f}^2$ leaderboard to catalyze research on this important problem. Our work has been presented at CVPR 2023.

a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across the vast dimensions of PES requires an unreasonably large number of preparations. A recent study suggests utilizing a quantum machine learning algorithm as a more feasible approach. This model utilizes quantum data from various phases of nuclear interactions to interpolate the ground-state geons throughout the few-nuclei region and project ground-state correlations across the entire PES. Notably, this approach has successfully achieved significant results with a minimal amount of training data. With just around 100 geometric nuclear configurations, this model has dramatically reduced the number of required preparations by several orders of magnitude and accurately predicts nuclear binding energies and radii with remarkable precision across the entire few-nuclei region. These findings suggest that nuclear structure might be effectively modeled using quantum machine learning with minimal nuclear data and these results also have implications for applications in the larger-scope nuclear interactions.

We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph satisfies the PMH-property or E2F condition, and find that there exist infinitely many papillon graphs that satisfy the PMH-property or E2F condition.

Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields.

A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. omechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture this phenomenon, new constitutive models have been developed, but their numerical solution remains challenging due to the nonlinear and irreversible nature of the underlying processes. In particular, modeling the irreversible transition of amorphous material into crystalline polymer requires specialized formulations and solution techniques. In response to these complexities, a new formulation has been derived based on the Holton model, suitable for numerical implementation using standard mixed finite element formulations. An efficient solution technique has also been proposed, consisting of a decoupled scheme and a mixed finite element approximation of the evolution equation for crystallinity. Numerical experiments have been conducted to validate and test the stability of the proposed scheme under various levels of time step and mesh refinement.

A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used computational models to analyze and visualize the concentration distribution of aerosols and heat within a bus over the course of one hour, considering possible infections caused by COVID-19, seasonal influenza, and other diseases. Our simulations revealed that sneezing produces a cooling plume of aerosols, which eventually warms up due to heat released from occupants, causing the aerosols to rise and concentrate near the ceiling of the bus. Notably, we found that mixing driven by coughing and sneezing outweighs the effects of ventilation on reducing aerosol concentration, resulting in higher concentrations near the top of the bus than at ground level. Furthermore, we observed a significant decrease in virus-laden aerosol concentration (approximately 10-fold) following a sneeze or cough within one hour, in comparison to the case without ventilation, indicating the importance of ventilation systems, such as HEPA filters and natural convection, in mitigating virus transmission. These insights offer valuable recommendations for optimizing ventilation to minimize virus transmission in enclosed spaces.

unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly perfect copy of the original message is as difficult for the adversary as producing any meaningful copy. Our findings build upon the previous construction and demonstrate that reaching any copy with even a minimal bit of information about the original message poses significant challenges for the adversary.

  - Beyond Bit Security: We've explored the possibility of enhancing the previous unclonable encryption construction founded on minimal assumptions to ensure security against any form of copy, rather than just those consisting of a single bit. Our research presents both private-key and public-key constructions that satisfy this improved security requirement, building upon the previous construction founded on minimal assumptions.

This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  This paper proposes a novel algorithm named SingleGAN that effectively generates high-quality multi-label data from this single positive annotation based a new modeling technique and a novel penalty term.  Experimental results demonstrate that SingleGAN outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of generation quality and its ability to satisfy complex multi-condition queries on a public dataset.  This single positive scenario is a more realistic setting that paves the way for the application of conditional GANs in industries, such as journalism.

high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.

Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration.

Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies.

This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually give way to sudden population shifts, resulting in SMMCs. However, these patterns disrupt the use of traditional methods for detecting EWIs in this scenario. To address this, we develop a novel indicator to detect the boundaries between ST and MMCOs, surpassing the limitations of the singular model.

Deep learning models are capable of automatically extracting these hidden features. However, such models often inadvertently learn to predict other information present in the images' metadata.
This information, which is often unrelated to surgery outcomes, includes the date when the scan was performed, the patient's age, and the type of cancer they have.
These embedded correlations can lead to spurious associations between these features and the surgery outcomes.
For example, newer cancer types are more likely to be diagnosed in younger patients, and these diagnoses are associated with better outcomes.
As such, deep learning models are prone to being biased by these complex relationships.
Our research investigates the development of fair X-ray images metadata-embedded representations.
In order to predict the metadata fields, we trained multiple supervised machine learning models and used them to identify these fields' representations that are highly correlated with the surgery outcomes.
Our approach involves identifying the parts of the representations that are less correlated with the metadata fields while maintaining their high correlation with the surgery outcomes.
Our solution is demonstrated on a dataset of breast cancer X-ray images and shows significant improvements in fairness metrics (up to 27% improvement in F1-score) with minimal loss in accuracy (at most 1.5% loss in accuracy) when compared to standard representations.

During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an even number of identical input variables or are even in nature.

A key finding is that the simple PTAS approach is not adequate for constraints that do not meet this criterion, such as 3-SAT. Instead, a more complex algorithm known as PCP is used to create a list of permitted constraint configurations.

Finally, the paper shows that the shattering method can be combined with the PCP to achieve a PTAS for CSPs on graph classes with limited connectivity and arbitrary constraints, as long as they meet specific criteria.

Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their faster rotation rates during their main sequence phase, even developing a differential rotation pattern similar to the Sun's. However, the 11 Solar Mass star, now evolved into a giant, exhibits a unusual core that is rotating four to five times faster than the Sun's core. Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data.

This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our astrobot simulation and timing simulation provide an efficient framework for evaluating astrobot performance and scheduling optimization techniques. Several methods to optimize the positioning of astrobots in both one and two dimensions are tested and compared, including methods to find optimal configurations in a single dimension as well as more complex two-dimensional arrangements. The most successful method to position astrobots involves dividing the target sky area into grid cells with a pre-determined size and determining the required spectrum and fiber coordinates for each cell. Several techniques to assign targets to templates are evaluated, including methods to divide the sky into equal areas, methods to divide the sky based on the probability of finding supernovae, and a method to construct a tree structure based on the position of the astrobots. The most effective technique to schedule astrobots involves assigning targets to templates based on a "supernova priority" method and then using a tree-based method to determine the order in which templates should be scheduled. These methods are suitable for addressing the scheduling requirements of the spectroscopic survey SDSS-V.

Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This alternative description is valid when the wavelength of light is significantly larger than the size of the unit cell, which is typically the case. However, it fails to accurately represent OTEs due to the infinite nature of the electromagnetic field. We propose that the dipole-based model can be viewed as a high-frequency approximation of the more comprehensive velocity-based model. The discrepancy between the two models yields an intuitive understanding of OTEs. We illustrate this with examples from dielectrics and topological insulators, as well as discussions on the limitations of the dipole-based model.

holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network frameworks based on the incorporation of distinct generators - those generating qubits and those qudits with higher degrees of freedom but lacking the ability to correct for erasure errors - which exhibit the desired characteristic of power-law behavior in the network's diameter relative to the distance between boundary nodes. Notably, this relationship relies on the incorporation of high-degree generators that can induce non-local correlations within the network, thereby influencing the calculation of physical properties as a function of the network's geometry.

This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing.

When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and an unyielding bureaucracy. This situation was compounded when van Rhijn's attempt to rekindle the lab's involvement in the broader astronomical community was thwarted in the 1950s due to his reluctance to collaborate with the newly formed Netherlands Institute for Astronomy. Ultimately, van Rhijn's legacy was further obscured when the lab was dismantled during the 1960s revolutions in astronomical research, leading to the decline and eventual disappearance of the Selected Areas Plan.

The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$.

This study's results are encouraging for future legged robots to safely navigate diverse and changing terrains.

A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter leads to a variation in parallax measurements, which can be expressed as $\delta \pi \approx \gamma \frac{1-c^2}{c^2} \pi$. Computational simulations of astrometry with variable PPN $\gamma$ confirmed these results, showing that even small deviations from $\gamma=1$ can have significant effects on parallax measurements. two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems in the form of Airy waves, but these waves exhibit poor localization. This concise analysis presents a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models which can accurately predict the existence of self-accelerating solitons. One such model, featuring interacting 1D solitons, involves a binary BEC trapped within an optical lattice consisting of one deep site and two shallow sites. This model utilizes a deep-site atom-reshaping resonant light to induce coupling and shape control of the solitons. Another model uses spatial modulation of a technical nonlinearity in light-matter interactions with an optical field in the form of a red-dressed atomic ensemble. This model introduces non-Hermitian effects that can be manipulated to adjust the acceleration of the resulting solitons, allowing for precise control over their dynamics.

a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that balances the need to visit nodes with similar data to the global distribution and minimizes communication with the server. A novel random walk learning algorithm is introduced and compared to traditional methods, demonstrating similar convergence rates while significantly reducing communication with the server and enhancing model accuracy.

To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold.

To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance system security while adhering to constraints on total power, bit rate requirements, and fading conditions. By utilizing convex optimization techniques and safe region concepts, we can develop efficient power allocation methods for both scenarios. Specifically, we propose a reliable security optimization method based on iterative subgradient steps for single-user systems, and an approach involving convex relaxation and mixed integer programming for multi-user/relay systems. We then compare the effectiveness of these methods through numerical examples and demonstrate their potential to provide secure and efficient wireless communication.

In photonic configurations, these edge currents translate to stable multi-mode waveguides that naturally protect the topological properties of the system. In our research, we combine these photonic setups with quantum sources, using a Harper-Hofstadter model to illustrate scenarios where quantum emitters display nearly quantized emission rates. These increased emission rates can result from interactions with multiple edge modes within different energy gaps. Notably, we find that spontaneous emission from these sources can separate spatially, creating time-bin qubits from single photons emitted into distinct non-degenerate modes. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of creating entanglement between emitters via their photons. Our work opens up the possibility of utilizing topological photonics structures as platforms for developing robust quantum technologies.

virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying general knowledge. However, creating these tests manually is time-consuming and labor-intensive. Unsupervised method offers a potential solution by automatically generating tests through natural language models. Current approaches rely on pre-trained models that have been trained on large datasets containing human-agent interactions. These models can produce reasonable dialogues when prompted with specific tasks or scenarios. We examine the state-of-the-art unsupervised testing methods and highlight their shortcomings: they fail to generate tests without extensive human knowledge or interaction data. Our research team developed an unsupervised natural language test generator for a complex knowledge-based virtual agent. This innovative approach consists of two novel components: an open-ended dialog generator based on the ProGPT2 model that allows for human interaction to provide context, and a set of transformation templates that refine the generated text based on the desired task or scenario. We compared the performance of our generated tests against human-written tests in a popular text-based adventure game, and found that our unsupervised method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art unsupervised testing methods in terms of agent performance.

Memory (LSTM) have been highly successful in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models are up to seven times more accurate than existing compressed LSTM models when applied to video recognition tasks. Furthermore, the hardware implementation of FDHT-LSTM achieves significant improvements in performance, power efficiency, and model size compared to conventional LSTM networks.

However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. This study provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings, encompassing an overview of methods such as token-level and sentence-level augmentations, along with experiments conducted on 11 datasets across topics/news classification, inference, paraphrasing, and single-sentence tasks. Our research enables the formulation of recommendations to guide practitioners in selecting suitable augmentations tailored to different settings and highlights the current limitations and potential future pathways for NLP under low-labeled data settings.

Another approach posits its fundamental expression as a statement regarding the number of ultraviolet degrees of freedom needed to realize the most highly charged black hole. This second interpretation becomes especially relevant in the context of generalized gravity theories, particularly those with an inverted sign for the gravitational constant. In such theories, a sufficiently highly charged black hole experiences repulsive forces from its electric field, overriding the attractive force of gravity. We explore a scenario where the WCConjecture is formulated as an upper limit to the charge of a stable, extremal black hole in generalized gravity theories. We investigate this conjecture for specific models including Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton-Axion theory and Skewon-Dilation theory. Our explorations reveal that the WCConjecture is satisfied for these models. We anticipate this to hold true for a broader class of generalized gravity theories.

on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE (MSQITE) expands on the original concept of using orthogonal states to create a model space and applies the evolution operator within that space. We explore the evaluation of excited states in two scenarios: directly calculating eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian and obtaining energy levels below the ground state by unitary down-mapping. Our analysis reveals that directly computing excited states is generally more efficient than the down-mapping method. In addition, we examine how choosing larger model spaces can lead to energy lowering but also require increased classical computation, potentially counterproductively.

the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In contrast, if the polynomial's derivative is not divisible by the prime p, the Galois group is isomorphic to an (n-folded, twisted) product of the symmetric group S_d.

Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies achieved varying surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films using low energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, which led us to a key finding - depending on the terminations, the metal-insulator transition may be significantly impeded or totally hindered near the surface due to distinct variations in electron distribution at different layers and altered screening length as compared to the bulk.  A considerable reorganization of spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition has also been observed, with an observable transfer of spectral weight across the entire energy scale from the high-binding energy regime to the low-binding energy regime, in contrast to our findings of unconserved total spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition, which indicates a failure in applying'sum rules of spectral weight',  a hallmark of systems with strong correlations.  Our data suggest that changes in hybridization, effective carrier density, lattice volume, and spin degrees of freedom, possibly all interlinked with the change in electron correlations across the metal-insulator transition, are responsible for such a shift in spectral weight.  Furthermore, our research demonstrates that in V$_2$O$_3$, the metal-insulator transition is fundamentally driven by correlation, and therefore, similar transitions in other systems may also involve the transfer of spectral weight

We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics, and that states with high condensate fractions should be well-represented by a quasi-condensation state that follows a mean-field model.

Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation.

This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This method diverges from conventional arithmetic product applications in configuration spaces, instead leveraging the geometric properties of Riemannian spaces to accommodate polynomial degrees of freedom within dual spaces. By exploiting the structure of elasticity problems, we establish a divergence-free property for the approximated displacement fields, which eliminates the need for a discrete Lagrange multiplier to enforce this constraint. Our approach is applicable to diverse boundary conditions, including Dirichlet and Neumann conditions, and avoids additional interpolations for the displacement field by representing the traction condition entirely in terms of the stress field. Notably, this method achieves $O(h^{k-1})$ convergence for general R in the $H^1$ norm, which, despite appearing to be $O(h^{k-1})$, can result in convergence rates of $O(h^2)$ or even $O(h^3)$ for popular polynomial orders.

By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in ODMR resonance broadening. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. Researchers have lately shown substantial interest in explosive synchronization phenomena which enable sudden shifts between these states due to their rapid and drastic nature. Although previous studies have highlighted key attributes of complex systems capable of explosive synchronization, these analyses were primarily undertaken on a case-by-case basis. This work establishes an exact standard for identifying explosive synchronization within coupled oscillator ensembles by determining the critical relationship between disorder in their internal workings and structure. This breakthrough brings us closer to understanding the intricacies of complex systems responsible for abrupt transitions and dual stability in both living organisms and man-made systems.

safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying CNN models. Despite the convenience offered by fast inference using stochastic neural network inference, training such reliable models remains a significant challenge. This is particularly evident when models are deployed in novel environments with diverse and unusual data. Existing techniques for robust training often fail in such scenarios. To overcome this obstacle, we introduce a new method called Variational Distilled Uncertainty Mapping, which leverages both the natural variability within neural network outputs and the power of generative models to generate diverse synthetic data. This unique combination enables our technique to map and reduce model uncertainty in critical network components, resulting in a more reliable model capable of resisting spoofing attacks and correctly identifying real faces in new environments.

netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy, affecting transactions and business-to-business interactions. Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual payment process can be substituted with a direct settlement. In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that existing computer systems can calculate four distinct netting solutions, offering various levels of financial security, and delay reductions compared to the baseline scenario.

Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. This specific boundary overlaps with another critical boundary that involves nonnegative polynomials and is characterized by polynomials that become zero at at least one point. Our focus lies on a separate part of the boundary that involves positive polynomials and doesn't overlap with points where the polynomial equals zero. 

For degree four, all such polynomials that break down into the sum of squares were recently identified by Marshall, but this breakdown was still recent and not entirely clear. We aim to split the boundary into two parts based on the degree of the polynomial's "index zero critical points" and provide a more accessible characterization of the critical points. 

Specifically, we show that the boundary between positive and nonnegative polynomials for degree four corresponds to the set of polynomials with at least one critical point at zero and specific geometric properties. We also provide an example to illustrate the complexity of the boundary and its relationship with other algebraic varieties. 

Our work also includes a broader analysis of the boundary's dimension and co-dimension for different degrees and shows that there are infinitely many distinct components of the boundary for degrees six through ten and no component that crosses odd degrees.

Due to limited access to the expertise of medical specialists, especially those dealing with rare cancers, computer-based systems have been developed to aid in these professionals' tasks. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. A straightforward examination indicates that this 1.5 order formalism is inherently defective in all contexts. limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical plasma that can alter the polarization of short high-power laser pulses. We demonstrate through simulations that our component, consisting of a thin layer of plasma, can convert linear polarization to circular polarization with high efficiency, even when the laser pulse intensity is in the terawatt range. We also find that this conversion process is relatively robust, resulting in minimal energy loss and an output polarization that exceeds the thresholds for laser damage in solid-state materials. This magnitude and scale of functionality, combined with its operation under high-power conditions, allows us to conclude that this plasma waveplate has immense potential for practical applications in high-power laser systems, and should be regarded as a viable alternative to traditional solid-state waveplates.

Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, we analyzed the optimal method to extract the primordial signal along with the lensing signal from $C_\ell^{EE}$ and $C_\ell^{BB}$ spectra. By generalizing quadratic estimators through the use of maximum a posteriori estimation, we derived the optimal lensing estimator and found that it outperforms the traditional method, especially in cases with higher lens amplitude. We also discovered that an optimal estimator that combines information from different multipoles performs the best, however such optimal estimators are computationally expensive, thus delensing algorithms that are nearly as effective but more feasible are needed. To bridge this gap, we presented an adaptive iterative Bayesian estimator that not only uses more efficient prior distributions, but also outperforms conventional methods, with only a small performance loss of about two percent in certain cases. This new approach could potentially enable higher precision measurements of the primordial gravitational waves in the coming years, as the accuracy of future experiments such as the Cosmic Microwave Background Stage IV will allow.

A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. avitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from neutron star mergers. Our project presents results from applying advanced neural network models to synthetic gravitational wave data representing binary neutron star and binary black hole events, which were generated using general relativistic hydrodynamics simulations. These neural networks, specifically a two-layer multi-layer perceptron and a Transformer, are evaluated for their capacity to distinguish between the two types of events, as well as to determine the mass of any neutron star involved. We find that both model types can successfully discriminate between the two types of events even in the presence of significant noise, with simple multi-layer perceptrons outperforming both the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo detector configurations, with a detection efficiency of approximately 95% and 70%, respectively. Furthermore, multi-layer perceptrons also demonstrate the ability to accurately predict neutron star mass.

However, acquiring high-quality, large-scale clinical data is complicated by data inconsistencies, formatting issues, and the fragmentation across multiple systems.  To tackle this challenge, we explored using Natural Language Processing (NLP) to integrate clinical data from Hospital Electronic Health Records (EHRs).  To do this, NLP techniques must first identify and extract metadata from various sources, such as Electronic Lab Reports (ELRs), radiology reports, progress notes, and discharge summaries. Our results showed that our NLP-based integration system could accurately identify test names, patient demographics, and lab values in ELRs with an average precision of 0.9. Our research provides an effective framework for clinical data extraction and integration, opening up new possibilities for NLP-based models to analyze complex clinical data and inform clinical decision-making.

To address these concerns, a systematic approach is outlined to numerically evaluate downlink 5G exposure among children, adolescents, schools, and medical centers. This methodology involves using a large-scale network simulation to generate an extensive dataset of 5G network configurations. , has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach is highly versatile and can be adapted to a variety of applications, making it an ideal platform for developing high-performance parallel applications.  Through extensive benchmarking and comparison with leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators using four SMMO applications, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance.

Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-rotating, fully-diffusive stellar interiors. While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.
