AR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. Within a solar-sized plasma experiment, we have discovered an new type of electromagnetic wave packet that had not been observed before. These wave packets are formed through the interaction of plasma particles with lower-hybrid wave packets and last for several plasma gyro-periods. Where lower-hybrid wave packets are produced within the plasma, they can lead to the formation of these new wave packets. Studies have revealed three key hallmarks of these new wave packets, including the conversion of kinetic energy into the electric field, the localization of lower-hybrid wave packets at the plasma center, and the formation of electron holes. As they move across the magnetic field lines, these new wave packets can potentially trigger the entry of plasma particles into the magnetic field, which could lead to further lower-hybrid wave packet formation.

Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique OVERWIND. Simulation results demonstrate that VSSA enhances the accuracy of tissue displacement estimation, particularly in the lateral direction, leading to more reliable overwind paths.

Our approach divides the expansive state space into smaller grids, where we computationally assess the probability of evasives being captured within each grid cell. By utilizing these capture likelihood values as revised reward signals, we can solve a deterministic equivalent game at a coarser resolution, obtaining a strategy for the active agents to navigate between grids. This process is repeated iteratively, generating a hierarchical network of graphs that a reinforcement learning agent can leverage to execute the fine-grained policy. We establish the theoretical basis for this hierarchy, showing that increasing the fidelity of the bottom layer ensures convergence to an optimal solution. We validate our hypothesis with a grid-world simulation and demonstrate its efficacy in a physical robot experiment.

A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a major limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have developed a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to reversing this process, utilizing the same data it initially had. By training just one generator, we are able to significantly reduce the requirements for both computational power and memory. In experiments on the 351-subject PROstate MARk (PROSMAR) dataset, our approach has shown promising results, achieving a high structural similarity (SSIM) of 0.877 and a high frequency similarity (FS) of 0.503, outperforming the original cycleGAN method by a noticeable margin.

screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods.

Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion.

we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

The task of polyp characterization involves analyzing the features of adenomas and advanced lesions to guide medical professionals in making informed clinical decisions. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved diagnostic accuracy, including lesion detection, segmentation, and classification. Nevertheless, existing models lack interpretability, hindering medical professionals from trusting and utilizing their predictions in clinical settings. Our project aims to develop an integrated pipeline for polyp characterization based on interpretable deep neural networks. Initially, we employ a network to classify images into different lesion types. Next, we select network nodes that contribute most to the classification decision and map them back to image regions using a reverse propagation method. This allows clinicians to visually see the most relevant parts of the input image that influenced the network's classification decision. Our results indicate that our proposed pipeline offers enhanced classification accuracy and more meaningful visualizations compared to existing methods.

This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios.

The higher water content found in pyroxene minerals from Benenitra and Chelyabinsk chondrites suggests that the parent bodies of these meteorites contained more water, in contrast to previous studies which indicated lower water contents.

By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech recognition. While zero-shot translation is highly promising, it's still in its nascent stages and faces challenges, notably speech normalization. We investigate two primary strategies to manage speech normalization: data harmonization and normalization harmonatization. We find that these strategies outperform zero-shot translation models trained on mixed data, which struggle to capture speaker characteristics. Notably, we introduce a new strategy called "separate normalization" that achieves significant improvements, resulting in -2.9 BLEU score improvement over combined normalization and an 8.7 BLEU improvement over current state-of-the-art.

, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths, which are directly influenced by neutrino mass eigenvalues. Through detailed tree and loop level analyses, we determine the parameters necessary to explain both dark matter annihilation within the sun's core via t-channel interaction and the correct relic abundance, as well as neutrino mass. Furthermore, we explore the connections and implications of these solutions within the extended Standard Model.

By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails.

In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that can accurately produce X-rays marked as normal or abnormal. Furthermore, our research showcased the ability to manipulate anatomical features within X-rays, all while maintaining their diagnostic authenticity. The successful completion of these tasks relied on a unique representation of medical features derived from radiological reports.

For domains with irregular boundaries, calculating these potentials in separate inner and outer areas is necessary. Existing high-order methods for evaluating these potentials involve transforming the domain to a standard shape through boundary or body-fitting techniques. However, these methods become overly complex for domains with intricate boundaries. In this research, a new approach is presented that directly addresses these regions using an unstructured grid. The method uses an expansion based on global orthogonal polynomials in the entire plane to represent the Newtonian potential, separately for areas inside and outside the domain's boundary. This new approach was tested on various shapes, including circular and distorted circles, and shows promising competitive when compared to established methods.
